::: {.tldr}
A good assistant remembers. **Long-term memory** lets an agent keep facts, past decisions and learned instructions **across conversations**. It comes in three kinds, borrowed from how human memory works: **semantic** (facts), **episodic** (experiences) and **procedural** (how to behave).
:::

## Short-term vs long-term

| | Short-term memory | Long-term memory |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | One conversation (one `thread_id`) | All conversations of a user |
| Mechanism in LangGraph | Checkpointer (the message history) | **Store** (a searchable database of memories) |
| Example | "What about LA?" after asking about SF | "Jim is my friend", remembered next week |

## The three types of memory

::: {.concepts}
::: {.concept}
`Semantic`: facts

What the agent knows about people, places and things. Like knowledge learned from a textbook. *"Jim is John's friend."*
:::
::: {.concept}
`Episodic`: experiences

Specific past events and actions, usually fed back as **few-shot examples**. *"Last time an email like this was ignored."*
:::
::: {.concept}
`Procedural`: skills

Instructions on how to behave. For an agent, this is mostly **the system prompt**. *"Always sign emails John Doe."*
:::
:::

## Choosing the right type

| The agent needs… | Use |
|---|---|
| Facts about people, places or things | **Semantic** memory |
| Concrete examples of the right decision | **Episodic** memory |
| Better instructions | **Procedural** memory |

## When to write memories

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  subgraph Hot["Hot path"]
    A1[Agent] -->|"writes memory<br/>while answering"| S1[(Store)]
  end
  subgraph BG["Background"]
    A2[Agent] --> R[Reply]
    A2 -.->|"conversation"| M[Memory manager]
    M -->|"writes later"| S2[(Store)]
  end
```

| | Hot path | Background |
|---|---|---|
| How | The agent saves memories itself while it responds | A separate process (often a second agent) updates memory afterwards |
| Pros | Simple, memories available immediately | Faster replies, clear separation of concerns |
| Cons | More work for the agent, slower replies | Two agents to manage, memories arrive with a delay |

## The course project: an email assistant

The course builds one assistant and adds a memory type at each step:

1. **Baseline**: a triage step (ignore / notify / respond) and a response agent with email and calendar tools.
2. **Semantic memory (hot path)**: the response agent gets tools to save and search facts.
3. **Episodic memory**: past triage decisions become few-shot examples in the triage prompt.
4. **Procedural memory (background)**: the prompts themselves are rewritten from user feedback.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Remember
- Short-term memory = one thread. Long-term memory = across threads, kept in a **store**.
- **Semantic** = facts, **episodic** = examples, **procedural** = instructions.
- Hot path = simple and immediate. Background = fast and clean, but delayed.
- These patterns apply to any agent, not just email.
:::

## Quiz

<details class="quiz">
<summary>An agent keeps using the wrong tone in its emails. Which memory type should you work on?</summary>
<p>Procedural memory: the instructions in its prompt need to change.</p>
</details>

<details class="quiz">
<summary>What is the main downside of updating memory in the hot path?</summary>
<p>The agent has more to do while answering, so it is slower and its job is more complex.</p>
</details>

<details class="quiz">
<summary>How do few-shot examples relate to episodic memory?</summary>
<p>They are past experiences (an input and the right decision) shown to the model so it repeats the same kind of decision.</p>
</details>
